summary: Give the PCB Trace Width calculator the ambient temperature, the trace width, the trace temperature and the voltage drop and it returns cross section. It is built for whatever you happen to be working on. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the PCB Trace Width calculator work?
sections.html:
The PCB Trace Width calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cross section in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the ambient temperature, the trace width (W), the trace temperature and the voltage drop.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in thou, thousandth of an inch. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the PCB Trace Width calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Cross section=(max. current ÷ (the trace is... × (max. desired temperature rise ^ 11 ÷ 25)), 40 ÷ 29)
Max. desired temperature rise=-ambient temperature + trace temperature
Trace thickness (t)=(500 ÷ 689) × ((max. current ÷ (the trace is... × (max. desired temperature rise ^ 11 ÷ 25)), 40 ÷ 29)) ÷ trace width (W)
Length=(100000000000 ÷ 17) × resistance × ((16129 ÷ 2500000000) × ((max. current ÷ (the trace is... × (max. desired temperature rise ^ 11 ÷ 25)), 40 ÷ 29))) ÷ (39 × trace temperature + 9025)
Max. current=voltage drop ÷ resistance
Resistance=power dissipation ÷ (max. current ^ 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Length, opening in fluid ounces per square foot
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in thou, thousandth of an inch
  • Area, opening in square mils
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The PCB Trace Width calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the ambient temperature, the trace width and the trace temperature — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the PCB Trace Width calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cross section, derived from the ambient temperature, the trace width and the trace temperature. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the PCB Trace Width calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the ambient temperature, the trace width, the trace temperature and the voltage drop, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter max. current in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Max. current opens in amperes and the chip beside it offers 3 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the PCB Trace Width calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
